Decision Trees¶

Description¶

In this practical we will experiment with Decision Trees using the existing implementation on scikit-learn. We will be exploring a classic dataset in Machine learning called "Iris Dataset". If you want to know more about the dataset you can find it at the following link (actual data, feature names).

The aim of this practical is twofold: first, to familiarise yourselves with the scikit framework and the many capabilities it has to offer in terms of manipulating data, and applying training algorithms. Second, you will be able to apply the knowledge you acquired regarding features, overfitting/underfitting and...well Decision Trees, obviously!

SUPER IMPORTANT NOTE: The documentation is your friend. Find out more about the Decision Trees implementation on scikit-learn here and here.

Exercise 1 - Dataset Analysis¶

Let's first do all the necessary imports and load the iris dataset using scikit. Then try to answer/implement the following questions (you don't have to write a report).

Note: Refrain from looking at the documentation for iris (yeah I know...) to find the answers, and instead use your numpy expertise on manipulating the arrays X and y. All you need to know is that X contains the examples (rows hold the examples, columns the features), and y has the labels for each example. feature_names, as the name of the variable implies, is an array with the names of each feature.

Note 2: You can also use Pandas as well to answer the following questions simply by importing X, y and feature_names.

  1. How many features does the dataset have?
  2. How many examples are there in the dataset?
  3. How many classes does the dataset have? What are they? (Hint: use the method iris.target_names)
  4. What are the types of the features?
  5. Compute the mean and standard deviation of the first two features.

X = iris.data
y = iris.target
feature_names = iris.feature_names

Excercise 2 - Train Decision Trees¶

Ok, we know a little bit now how our features look like. Next, let's go ahead and train a Decision Tree. We will be using an implementation that only handles numeric values (luckily iris only has numeric values, otherwise we would have to convert binary and categorical to 1-of-k representations).

We will be using sklearn.tree.DecisionTreeClassifier which has many more hyperparameters than we have seen in the Theory part (yes, it's an advanced production-ready code). The two most interesting hyperparamters you need to care about are the criterion and the max_depth.

For the first one, scikit-learn uses two slightly more sophisticated scoring functions (namely Gini impurity (default) and Information Gain (entropy)), than the one we have seen in Theory. You can find more information here. Leave it to the default setting (criterion="gini"), and you can experiment with it later if you have time.

We mostly care about max_depth because we know that this is our key to controlling the complexity of the final decision tree (i.e., how many questions to ask), hence controllling overfitting and underfitting.

Finally, after 3 weeks of waiting, we are ready for some real action! Let's see how we can:

  • Train a decision tree with max_depth=1.
  • Predict the class of the 10th example.
  • Predict the class for all examples in the training set.
  • Compute the training accuracy.

SUPER IMPORTANT NOTE: Go through each of the lines ONE-by-ONE and try to understand what each step does!!!

In [6]:
# set max_depth
depth=1
#dt = tree.DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth)
dt= tree.DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="entropy", max_depth=3)
# Train on data
dt.fit(X, y)

# predict class on the 10th example
# Notice how we reshape the 10th row of X. This is necessary as predict expects a 1-d array, 
# i.e., shape (1,N), rather than a vector. 
# NOTE: Try without reshaping and see what will happen.
example_id = 10
pred_10 = dt.predict(X[10].reshape(1,-1))

# get the class name, just for fun!
pred_10_class = iris.target_names[pred_10[0]]

print("Prediction for example {} is {} and has class name: {}".format(example_id, pred_10, pred_10_class))
# Predict on the whole training set
preds = dt.predict(X)
# A very fancy way to compute training accuracy! (It can't get any more `Pythonic` that this :D )
# NOTE: What is `preds == y` really? Try to print it and check its shape...
train_acc = np.mean(preds == y)
print("Training accuracy: {:1.3f} for depth = {}".format(train_acc, depth))

# dt.predict(X[10])
print(X[10].shape)
print(X[10].reshape(1, -1).shape)

a = np.ones((3,4))
print(a.shape)
print(a.reshape(1, -1).shape)

Exercise 3 - Plot Decision Trees¶

Let's try now to see what the actual Decision Tree looks like!

We will first train a model of depth=1 and then output the graph.

In [8]:
depth=10
#crt='entropy'
crt='gini'
dt = tree.DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion=crt, splitter='random', max_depth=depth)
# Train on data
dt.fit(X, y)    
plt.figure(figsize=(40,20))
_ = tree.plot_tree(dt, feature_names=iris.feature_names, class_names=iris.target_names, filled=True, rounded=True)
plt.show()

Exercise 4 - Decision Boundaries¶

This is optional, but very interesting. We will compute the decision boundaries (and the surfaces of the corresponding classes they separate into) for a trained model in 2D for all pairs of features. Here is how:

In [11]:
depth = 1

# Parameters
n_classes = 3
plot_colors = "ryb"
plot_step = 0.02
plt.figure(figsize=(10,10))

for pairidx, pair in enumerate([[0, 1], [0, 2], [0, 3],
                                [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3]]):
    # We only take the two corresponding features
    X = iris.data[:, pair]
    y = iris.target

    # Train
    dt = DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X, y)

    # Plot the decision boundary
    plt.subplot(2, 3, pairidx + 1)

    x_min, x_max = X[:, 0].min() - 1, X[:, 0].max() + 1
    y_min, y_max = X[:, 1].min() - 1, X[:, 1].max() + 1
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.arange(x_min, x_max, plot_step),
                         np.arange(y_min, y_max, plot_step))
    plt.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5, w_pad=0.5, pad=2.5)

    Z = dt.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
    Z = Z.reshape(xx.shape)
    cs = plt.contourf(xx, yy, Z, cmap=plt.cm.RdYlBu)

    plt.xlabel(iris.feature_names[pair[0]])
    plt.ylabel(iris.feature_names[pair[1]])

    # Plot the training points
    for i, color in zip(range(n_classes), plot_colors):
        idx = np.where(y == i)
        plt.scatter(X[idx, 0], X[idx, 1], c=color, label=iris.target_names[i],
                    cmap=plt.cm.RdYlBu, edgecolor='black', s=15)

plt.suptitle("Decision surface of a decision tree using paired features")
plt.legend(loc='lower right', borderpad=0, handletextpad=0)
plt.axis("tight")
plt.show()
